analysis.one_liner: Bars federal officials from profiting off their offices, ends taxpayer-funded travel to their own properties, and requires presidents to disclose tax returns.
analysis.headline: A Democratic anti-corruption package targeting presidential self-enrichment was referred to three House committees and died without a hearing, a vote, or a single Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make the President and other protected officials reimburse the Treasury for security and travel costs when they stay at hotels or resorts they own. It would ban federal funds for senior officials' private and chartered flights, create criminal penalties for using public office for private gain, require senior officials and their spouses to put major business holdings into blind trusts, and publish the President's tax returns, White House visitor logs, employee salaries, and financial disclosures. It would also bar the President, Vice President, and their immediate families from federal contracts or federal payments beyond their salary, and require reports whenever federal money flows to the President's businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently foot multimillion-dollar security and travel bills when the President visits his own properties; voters, who would get access to the President's tax returns, White House visitor logs, and staff financial disclosures; and the public generally, through new criminal penalties for self-dealing by senior officials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and voters seeking government transparency

how_it_helps.text: Officials protected by the Secret Service would have to reimburse the Treasury for protection and other government costs incurred when they stay at a hotel or resort in which they hold an ownership or financial interest.

Federal funds could no longer pay for senior political appointees to travel on private or chartered flights unless they certify no commercial flight was available, with false certification subject to criminal penalties.

Senior White House officials and Senate-confirmed appointees would face fines and up to five years in prison for using their office for private gain or coercing subordinates to benefit themselves, friends, or relatives.
Senior federal officers and their spouses would have to divest significant business interests into qualified blind trusts, enforceable by state attorneys general or any aggrieved person.

Presidents and major-party presidential nominees would have to publicly disclose three years of income tax returns, with the Office of Government Ethics and FEC empowered to obtain the returns from the Treasury if withheld.
Agencies would have to report federal spending at Trump Organization properties, and the Office of Management and Budget would report annually on direct and indirect ways federal money benefits them.
The President would have to report quarterly on White House security clearances, including anyone granted a clearance despite an unfavorable recommendation.
White House visitor logs, employee salaries, and employee financial disclosures would be published on a searchable public website.
The President, Vice President, and their immediate families could no longer hold federal contracts, leases, or grants or receive federal funds beyond their official salary.
Nepotism rules would be extended to the White House and Executive Office of the President, with violators removed immediately.

Agencies issuing major rules that financially benefit the President or senior advisors would have to quantify and publish that conflict of interest, and Congress would be notified of changes in inspectors general's status.

analysis.who_pays: The President, Vice President, and their immediate family members and businesses, which would lose federal payments, contracts, and the value of government spending at their properties, and would owe reimbursements for protection costs; senior officials, who would have to divest business holdings and give up private-jet travel; and federal agencies, which would bear the cost of the new reporting and disclosure requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Trump family, its businesses, and senior officials

drawbacks.text: The bill defines 'covered property' as property controlled by the Trump Organization, so several provisions single out one president's businesses by name rather than writing a general rule for all future presidents, which critics would call politically selective legislation.

Requiring a protected official to reimburse the Secret Service for protection costs treats security spending as a subsidy to the official's property choice, but protection follows the person rather than the venue, raising questions about how much of the cost the bill could actually recover and whether the reimbursement requirement could survive legal challenge.

Several provisions are reports or 'sense of the Congress' statements with no enforcement mechanism, and the judicial-review section bars the disclosure failures from being used to challenge or block any agency rule, limiting the teeth of the regulatory-conflict provisions.

Requiring divestiture by the spouses of senior officials goes beyond existing ethics law and would raise practical and privacy concerns about forcing family members to sell lawful assets as a condition of a relative's government service.

The charter-flight ban's 'no commercial flight available' exception is self-certified by the traveling official, the same loophole critics cited in past travel scandals like Administrator Pruitt's and Secretary Price's chartered flights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and documented cost to taxpayers — security, travel, and federal spending that flows to a president's private businesses — and would have created genuine transparency through tax returns, visitor logs, and clearance reporting. Its weaknesses are real: several of its most quotable provisions target one president's businesses by name rather than all future presidents, some provisions are reporting-only, and the family-divestiture and reimbursement requirements raise practical and legal questions. Even with those flaws, the core substance — penalties for self-dealing, blind trusts, disclosure of money flowing to the President's companies — is a legitimate response to documented practices, and the costs fall on the officials and businesses being regulated rather than on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late November 2018 and referred to three House committees, but none of them took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in early January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the Restoring the Public Trust Act on November 20, 2018, with four Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Committees on Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary, and Ways and Means, with no date set for consideration.
The bill's action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no further movement after the initial referral.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and all bills not passed by then die.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death left the status quo intact: the President's family businesses kept receiving federal spending and had no reimbursement obligation for protection costs at their own properties, and senior officials faced no new divestiture, disclosure, or self-dealing requirements. Senior administration officials and the Trump Organization were better off because it died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Trump Organization and senior administration officials

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Restoring the Public Trust Act and led its cosponsorship effort.

for.name: 4 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Reps. Cicilline, Eshoo, Gallego, and Sanchez).

against.name: Rep. Trey Gowdy
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the primary committee of referral, never brought the bill to a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for House floor action during the remainder of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled House, in its final weeks of the majority, took no action on the bill in any of its three committees.

industries.industry: Trump Organization (hotels, golf resorts, Trump Tower)
industries.note: Federal agencies, foreign governments, and the Secret Service were spending money at the President's properties, which the bill's findings describe as taxpayer subsidies to his businesses. The bill would bar most federal payments to those businesses and force reimbursement of protection costs, cutting off that revenue.

industries.industry: Private and chartered aviation serving federal officials
industries.note: The bill bans federal funds for senior officials' private or chartered flights, eliminating a market that drew public criticism when Cabinet secretaries used it. Commercial airlines' business would correspondingly gain.
